report:
Contrary to the initial belief, robust high-quality evidence indicates that arthroscopic surgery (joint endoscopy involving lavage or debridement) does **not** effectively improve outcomes for knee osteoarthritis compared to placebo or conservative management.

### The Evidence

* **Placebo-Controlled Trials:** A seminal trial in *The New England Journal of Medicine* demonstrated that knee arthroscopy provided no greater pain relief or functional improvement than a placebo (sham) surgical procedure (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259).
* **Systematic Reviews:** A comprehensive Cochrane review confirmed that arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease offers no clinically meaningful benefit over non-surgical care or sham surgery (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease).
* **Clinical Guidelines:** Major medical bodies, including the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS), explicitly recommend against arthroscopy with lavage or debridement for primary knee osteoarthritis (https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf).

### Why Was It Used?

Historically, clinicians believed that flushing out cartilage debris and inflammatory factors provided temporary relief (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4435528/). While arthroscopy may occasionally be considered for distinct secondary mechanical issues, such as true joint locking caused by loose body fragments, rigorous trials show it fails to treat osteoarthritis itself.

### Conclusion

High-level medical evidence demonstrates that knee arthroscopy does not provide significant clinical benefit for osteoarthritis. First-line management focuses instead on non-surgical treatments, such as physical therapy, exercise, weight management, and targeted pain relief.
